# Figure 4 Specification — Retrieval Effect of Repair with Bootstrap 95% CIs

**Status:** Evidence and specification only. No figure has been generated by this package.
**Canonical data:** `figure4_bootstrap_data.csv`, `figure4_ready_to_plot.csv` (this directory)
**Row order:** `forest_plot_order.csv` (this directory)

---

## Title

**Figure 4. Retrieval effect of preference-graph repair with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.**

## Scientific message

Repairing a preference graph's cycles (FAS repair) does **not** reliably improve downstream retrieval quality. Across 24 dataset × regime × method-pair combinations, 20 show exactly zero effect (repair inactive on near-acyclic graphs, or the balance hybrid is insensitive to repair even when the graph is cyclic). Of the 4 combinations where the graph is substantially cyclic (`ms1`) and the method is Copeland, only **one** — HotpotQA — shows a 95% CI that excludes zero, and it is positive. The dataset with the *lowest* ms1 cyclicity (51.9%, vs. 60–95% for the others) is the one where repair helps; the two more cyclic datasets (SciDocs, FiQA) do not show a reliable effect. This is the figure that operationalizes the manuscript's central claim: **structural graph consistency and downstream retrieval quality are decoupled.**

## Type of visualization

Forest plot: one horizontal row per (dataset, regime, method-pair), a point at the mean ΔnDCG@15, and a horizontal whisker spanning the 95% bootstrap CI.

## Axis labels

- **x-axis:** "ΔnDCG@15 (repaired − unrepaired)"
- **y-axis:** row labels of the form `{dataset} / {regime} / {pair}` (e.g. `hotpotqa / ms1 / copeland`); no numeric y-axis, categorical only.

## Reference line

Vertical dashed line at **x = 0**. This is the null-effect reference; CIs that do not cross it are the only rows licensed to be called "significant."

## Grouping

Two groups by `group` column in `figure4_ready_to_plot.csv`:
- **Copeland (repaired − unrepaired)** — 12 rows
- **Balance (repaired − unrepaired)** — 12 rows

Recommend rendering as two stacked panels (Copeland on top, Balance below) or two colors within one panel, since the Balance group is uniformly null and would otherwise visually crowd the x=0 line.

## Ordering

Use `forest_plot_order.csv` exactly (column `order`, ascending). Summary: dataset blocks ordered by descending ms1 cyclicity (FiQA → SciDocs → BRIGHT → HotpotQA, matching the established Figure 2 dataset order), regimes in natural order within each dataset block (ms2 → ms1 → ms1_drop_mutual), Copeland before Balance within each regime. HotpotQA is placed last deliberately so the one significant effect lands as the closing row of the plot.

Follow the palette already fixed elsewhere in the manuscript plan (`FIGURE_SPECIFICATIONS.md` global style, Okabe–Ito, colorblind-safe):

## Caption draft

> Figure 4. Bootstrap mean ΔnDCG@15 (repaired minus unrepaired hybrid ranking) with 95% confidence intervals (2,000 bootstrap resamples), for Copeland and balance hybrid rankings, across four benchmarks (SciDocs, FiQA, HotpotQA, BRIGHT) and three vote-extraction regimes (ms2, ms1, ms1_drop_mutual). Twenty of twenty-four rows show an interval of exactly [0, 0]: this includes every ms2 and ms1_drop_mutual row (near-acyclic graphs, where FAS repair removes negligible edge weight) and every balance-hybrid row regardless of regime. Among the four ms1/Copeland rows — the only combinations with substantial graph cyclicity (52–95% of queries) and a method sensitive to repair — only HotpotQA's interval excludes zero (mean Δ = +0.017, 95% CI [0, 0.041]); FiQA is directionally positive but its interval straddles zero, SciDocs is directionally negative with its interval straddling zero, and BRIGHT is effectively zero. Notably, HotpotQA has the lowest ms1 cyclicity rate (51.9%) of the four datasets, indicating that the severity of structural inconsistency does not predict the size or reliability of any retrieval benefit from repair.

## Expected interpretation

A reader should conclude: (1) repair is inactive by construction whenever the graph is already near-acyclic; (2) even when the graph is substantially cyclic, retrieval effects are heterogeneous and usually statistically indistinguishable from zero; (3) the one exception (HotpotQA ms1 Copeland) does not come from the most cyclic dataset, undermining any simple "more cycles → more benefit from repair" story; (4) the balance hybrid shows no retrieval sensitivity to repair in any cell tested.

## Reviewer takeaway

This figure is the paper's evidence that **a data-quality intervention that measurably improves structural consistency (Figure 3) does not reliably translate into improved retrieval quality** — the central decoupling claim of the JDIQ submission. Reviewers should not read this figure as "repair sometimes helps, sometimes hurts, roughly at random" — the effect is null in the large majority of cells by construction (repair had nothing to remove), and only genuinely uncertain (CI straddling zero) in the small remaining set of cyclic-and-method-sensitive cells, with exactly one exception. The figure is intentionally conservative: it reports CIs rather than point estimates alone, and does not claim significance where the interval crosses zero.
